summary: Data centers and other sites reach backbone networks through gateway routers, often several. This document uses the BGP Tunnel Encapsulation attribute to let gateways advertise routes to prefixes in the site, including on behalf of other gateways, so Segment Routing can identify multiple paths between gateways for load-balancing, resilience and quality.

eli5.summary: A building with several front doors needs a way to tell visitors about all of them. This document lets doors announce themselves so the best path can be chosen.

subtitle: How gateways to a data center find each other and advertise every route into the site, so segment routing can use all of them.

tldr.problem: A site with several gateways usually has only the single best BGP route to a prefix passed across the backbone, so remote sites cannot see all the gateways or balance traffic across them.
tldr.mechanism: Gateways discover each other through auto-discovery routes tagged with a shared site identifier in a route target. Each gateway then attaches to every route it advertises a Tunnel Encapsulation attribute holding the union of all the site's gateways.
tldr.outcome: Remote gateways see every entry point to the site, however the next hop changes, and can pick or balance SR paths for load-balancing, resilience and quality.

today: RFC 9125 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 9012, the BGP Tunnel Encapsulation attribute.

sections.title: Many Gateways, One Visible Route
sections.content:
Data centers (DCs) are linked by a backbone network of private networks and/or the Internet, and attach to it through gateways (GWs). One DC typically has more than one GW, for commercial preferences, load balancing or resilience. Other sites, such as access networks, are connected the same way.

A source site that uses Segment Routing (SR) must know the full set of entry GWs of the destination site to load-balance flows. The obvious source of that information, the next hop in a route, does not work: typically only the best route chosen by BGP is distributed across the backbone, which precludes load-balancing across both GWs.

BGP Add-Paths (RFC 7911) could distribute all routes, but the GW identity is lost once an ASBR sets itself as next hop, and with several ASes in the backbone Add-Paths runs into scaling issues. So it is effectively limited to sites connected over a single AS.
sections.eli5: If only the closest door is ever announced, visitors never learn the others exist. Telling them about every door lets them spread out.

sections.title: The Core Idea
sections.content:
The solution uses the BGP Tunnel Encapsulation attribute (RFC 9012). When a GW advertises a route to a prefix X in its site, it includes an attribute that is the union of the Tunnel Encapsulation attributes advertised by every GW to that site, itself included.

So the attribute carries multiple Tunnel TLVs, one or more per active GW, and each has a Tunnel Egress Endpoint sub-TLV naming that GW. Even if only one route reaches other ASes and the next hop changes many times, the attribute stays unchanged.

In the RFC's example, GW1 and GW2 discover each other and both advertise routes to X. Each includes the union of both attributes, so the ingress gateway sees all paths to X whichever route reaches it, and can choose one or balance flows.

The solution does not require the transit ASes to be SR-capable, but the GWs and ASBRs must be, since SR is used to stitch path segments between them. It can extend into the sites if they are SR-capable.
sections.eli5: Each door hands out a flyer listing all the doors, including itself. Whichever flyer reaches you, you know every way in.

sections.title: Site Gateway Auto-Discovery
sections.content:
GWs find each other with these rules.

  • A route target (RFC 4360) MUST be attached to each GW's auto-discovery route, with a value indicating the site identifier. A Type x00 or x02 route target is RECOMMENDED.
  • Site identifiers are configured. They MUST be the same on all GWs to a site and unique across all interconnected sites.
  • Each GW MUST import any route carrying a route target with its own site identifier, so all GWs to a site learn the current set of active GWs.

The auto-discovery route has two parts: IPv4 or IPv6 NLRI holding one of the GW's loopback addresses (AFI/SAFI 1/1, 2/1, 1/4 or 2/4), and a Tunnel Encapsulation attribute with the GW's encapsulation information in one or more Tunnel TLVs. The advertised address MUST differ from the loopback used for packets to the GW itself, to avoid applying the attribute to packets addressed to the GW.

When the set of active GWs changes, each externally advertised route is re-advertised with an updated attribute. A GW that loses its backbone connection or is retired MUST withdraw its advertisements.

A GW configured with the wrong site identifier is not discovered by the others and does not discover them. Remote sites would then see only the attribute from the BGP best route.
sections.eli5: Doors of the same building wear the same name badge. Each one only listens to doors with its badge, so they find each other. A door with the wrong badge gets left out.

sections.title: Using the Routes for SR Paths
sections.content:
A remote GW that receives a route to X uses the Tunnel Egress Endpoint sub-TLVs to identify the GWs through which X is reachable. It computes SR Traffic Engineering paths across the backbone using information from BGP-LS (RFC 9085), correlated by site identity. SR Egress Peer Engineering (RFC 9086) can add to the BGP-LS information.

A packet sent on an SR TE path into the egress site must carry the receiving GW's SID for X as the next SID to process. So each Tunnel TLV contains a Prefix-SID sub-TLV for X. That sub-TLV is only defined for IPv4/IPv6 Labeled Unicast routes, so the solution applies only to those route types.

Alternatively, with MPLS SR, if the GWs let remote sites steer through their site, each GW computes an SR TE path through its site to X and puts it in an MPLS Label Stack sub-TLV in the SR Tunnel TLV.

If a site allows remote GWs to send in its native encapsulation, each GW also includes a Tunnel TLV for that encapsulation, one per GW, each with a Tunnel Egress Endpoint sub-TLV giving the GW's address.
sections.eli5: Once you know every door, you can plan a route to the one you like, and the list also tells you the right password to give at that door.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The mechanisms rely on the security already defined for BGP. They share reachability information between sites, so security that depends on site boundaries is weakened. Exposures the RFC lists include these.

  • Anyone who snoops a site's BGP exchanges or subverts a gateway can learn the full set of gateways, which eases attacks on that site.
  • The existence of multiple gateways becomes visible across the backbone, so an attacker can target the whole set at once.
  • A node without external BGP peering might get itself advertised as a gateway by genuine gateways, and attract traffic.
  • A modified BGP message in the backbone could spoof a gateway and cause traffic to be misdelivered.

The RFC says these are new exposures of information rather than new protocol vulnerabilities, to be mitigated with existing mechanisms such as securing the TCP sessions that carry BGP. Operators MUST consider gateway-to-gateway encryption, and due consideration MUST be given to encrypting end-to-end traffic.

For management, the main new configuration item is the site identifier. It needs coordination, probably by a central management agent, and a misconfiguration stops gateways discovering each other. Operators should also consider the effect of Route Target Constraint (RFC 4684) filtering, which may be desirable or may limit the procedures.
sections.eli5: A list of all your doors is handy for visitors, but a burglar would like it too. So the list should travel in a locked bag.

sections.title: IANA Action
sections.content:
IANA maintains the registry of BGP Tunnel Encapsulation Attribute Tunnel Types. It had earlier assigned value 17 for "SR Tunnel", referencing this document as an Internet-Draft, when that range was First Come First Served.

IANA has marked that assignment as deprecated, and may reclaim the codepoint when the registry is depleted.
sections.eli5: A badge number was handed out early for this idea. It has now been retired and may be reused later.
